game.name: Inkshade
game.short_description: Inkshade is a turn-based tactics game carved out of strange wooden miniatures, wrapped in a web of locked rooms, and orchestrated by an otherworldly game master. Victory is not guaranteed, and the only constant is the cruel black ink that flows within the pieces.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Inkshade is an Inscryption-style game that swaps cards for pawns placed on a small tactical board. He loves the haunted-house exploration, narrator, story and puzzles outside combat, but found the combat itself boring and shallow. Strategy is limited, pieces are near-identical, and progress leans heavily on meta-progression stat upgrades. He finished it out of curiosity, describes the experience as mixed, and places it in low B, recommending it to Inscryption fans who can tolerate the gameplay.
praise: Out-of-combat vibe: a house that slowly opens up, with a narrator who guides and sometimes misleads you
Unlocking new rooms feels exciting, with puzzles that are solid
Story and mystery hold him in from start to finish
Spooky atmosphere, with some genuinely freaky moments
Combat boards look cool and each has a small story setup
Captures Inscryption's vibe, which is hard to replicate
criticism: Combat is boring: only movement and attack, with little strategy
Most pieces are nearly identical and enemies differ mainly in health, damage and range
Heavily dependent on meta-progression stat upgrades, so some fights are mathematically unwinnable without them
Dominant strategy is to buff a single unit and have it carry everything
No real builds during a run; fights are predictable from start to end and the same board repeats
Ending was less satisfying than hoped; low replayability as a one-time adventure
unique_points: Copies Inscryption's vibe without its card gameplay, which is harder to clone than typical mechanics
Only two damage and defense types (magical or physical)
Acts more like a one-time adventure than a replayable roguelike
commentary.quote: I can definitely recommend Inkshade as long as you're okay with the gameplay.
design_criteria: Strategy depth: combat has too few actions and options
Build variety: no builds beyond pre-run planning
Meta-progression: over-reliance on stat upgrades makes fights depend on them
Enemy design: enemies are near-identical beyond stats
Atmosphere and vibe: a major strength outside combat
Puzzles and exploration: rewarding room unlocks and puzzle design
Story and narrative: compelling mystery and narrator
Replayability: a one-time experience with modes afterward

community.one_liner: A first-person, dark-atmosphere turn-based tactics roguelite by Studio Vezelle where you command wooden board-game miniatures against a malicious game master, with locked-room escape puzzles between battles.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate Inkshade Very Positive (about 87% of roughly 636 reviews, Steam listing as of the data pull), driven by its atmosphere, sound and art, and the creepy, sardonic game master. The common caveat is that the tactics are shallow and the roguelite loop is grindy: units differ mostly by stats and a few broken-strong upgrade paths trivialise late fights. It is constantly compared to Inscryption, usually unfavourably on depth but favourably on vibe. There are no critic reviews: Metacritic has a page with zero critic reviews and only 2 user ratings, and no OpenCritic entry was found. The game is a finished 1.0 (not early access) that got several post-launch patches in Aug-Sep 2025 (lantern toggle, contrast slider, walk speed, new challenge mode), and still receives positive reviews into 2026.
best_things: Atmosphere, art direction, lighting and sound design (the wooden 'bonk' of pieces, battle themes, end-credits track) are the most consistently praised element
The game master is a memorable, sardonic and malicious narrator whose worldbuilding and banter give the run a sense of story
Escape-room style puzzle sections in locked rooms give a satisfying break from combat and several reviewers found them clever and tough
Tactical board is simple and readable: pieces cannot pass through each other, so bottlenecks, shielding and elevation matter
Collecting and upgrading new pieces feels rewarding, and tense battles where you could lose your whole roster give real dread
Strong Inscryption-like vibe with different mechanics (mid-run recruiting of defeated enemies, hex-grid tactics) that some find a fresh spin
Steam Deck works well per at least one reviewer (minor remapping), plus accessibility options like adjustable difficulty and colour alternatives
worst_things: Tactical depth is shallow: units are differentiated almost entirely by five stats (movement, health, range, damage, defense) and only a few have special abilities
Balance is exploitable: stacking armour/attack on one or two pieces (the Wretch is repeatedly named) makes most enemies and bosses trivial, so strategy falls away
Enemy AI is passive and only engages when a piece is in range, enabling simple luring tactics
Very dark visuals; even with lantern and brightness options, some players cannot see enemy units and felt unfairly killed
Performance and stability complaints: low fps on mid-range GPUs, some maps heavy, and one reviewer reported frequent crashes on an older Win10 PC (fine on a newer machine)
Controls can be clumsy: passing a unit's turn with a triple click is easy to trigger accidentally, no clear attack-range preview for ranged units before moving, unit names hard to see
The narrator talks a lot and dialogue cannot easily be skipped even after many repeats
Story and character connections are thin and the ending left some players unsatisfied; limited replayability after finishing
improvements: Add more unit abilities and build variety (area attacks, taunt, summons, status effects) so pieces differ beyond stat numbers
Rebalance upgrade costs and scaling so one maxed piece or armour stacking cannot trivialise the game, and so early grinding feels less punishing
Improve brightness/visibility and add camera options (decouple camera from mouse, manual camera toggle) to address eye strain and motion sickness
Fix the unit-pass input (allow un-passing or use a less accident-prone control) and show attack range and unit names more clearly
Let players skip or shorten repeated narrator dialogue
Optimise performance and stability, and consider modding/community map support or more backstory content (suggested by one reviewer)
unique_things: Combines first-person escape-room exploration of locked rooms and an airship setting with a turn-based tactics board game run by a hostile game master
Pieces are wooden miniatures on a physical-feeling board with hex grid, elevation and height effects
Roguelite meta-progression through spending scrip on permanent upgrades to a collected roster, plus a mid-run recruitment system for defeated enemies
A post-campaign challenge mode (including a Monomanipulation mode for single-unit runs added in Sep 2025) that players say is closer to a classic roguelite
Unlocking new pieces is tied to solving puzzle rooms, and opening rooms is tied to progressing through battles
tedious_or_disliked: Grind: you need upgrades to win fights and need to fight (and often lose) to earn upgrade currency; reviewers cite only about 15-20 scrip per failed run versus 50 for a single point of damage
Dying can send you back large sections, keeping pieces and upgrades but losing run progress, which feels heavy in mid/late game
Enemies and early encounters scale with progress, so knowledge and skill matter less than how many upgrades you bought
Spreading upgrades across many pieces is a trap; new players may have to restart or soft-lock themselves on harder settings after a reset
Long runs with repetitive combat and a chatty narrator during tutorial/first-hour failure scripting
Darkness and camera behaviour causing eye strain or motion sickness for some
divisive_points: Inscryption comparison: some see a worthy atmospheric cousin, others call it a shallow imitation without Inscryption's mechanical depth
Difficulty: some enjoy brutal early hours and tense fights, others find it grindy early and then trivial once an overpowered build is found
Puzzle rooms: praised as a highlight by some, called shallow or unclear by others
Narrator and story: charming and creepy to some, repetitive and flat to others
community.reception_notes: Released Aug 14, 2025 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux) at $19.99, developed and published by Studio Vezelle. Post-launch patches: The Lantern Update v1.1.010 (Aug 30, 2025) made the lantern toggleable and added a contrast slider and brightness button, directly responding to visibility complaints; v1.1.011 (Sep 6) added Monomanipulation challenge mode; v1.1.012 (Sep 17) added faster unit walk speed and fixed keymapping bugs. A soundtrack was released Sep 29, 2025. Reviews continue into 2026 and stay mostly positive. Metacritic had 0 critic reviews and only 2 user ratings at fetch time and no OpenCritic page was found, so there are no aggregate critic scores. SteamSpy-style owner data was not informative (0-20k), so copies sold is unknown; $193.9k estimated gross at roughly $12-20 average realised price implies on the order of 10-15k copies, which is my rough inference, not a sourced figure.
